5. The learned Munsif by his impugned judgment and order dated 4.4.85 disallowed pre-emption holding that the disputed transfer was a usufructuary mortgage and as such pre-emption is barred under section 96 sub-section 10(d) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Against aforesaid impugned Judgment and order the petitioner took an appeal before the District Judge, Kurigram being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 133 of 1985, and the learned Subordinate Judge, who heard the appeal, has been pleased by his impugned Judgment and order to dismiss the appeal upholding the judgment and order passed by the learned trial Court. 

 7. Mr. Munsur Habib, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor-petitioner, submits that regard been to the admitted fact that the disputed sale deed is evidently an out of out sale deed with condition embodied therein for re conveyance to the vendors, the learned Court of appeal below erred in law in treating a complete sale deed as a deed of usufructuary mortgage on an erroneous view of law regarding the import of section 96 sub-section 10(d) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the same has resulted in erred in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that in view of the fact that the case land has admittedly not as yet been a reconveyed to the original vendors in pursuance of the alleged unregistered deed of agreement; the learned Courts below evidently erred in law in treating a complete sale deed Ext. A as a deed of mortgage and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Advocate also submits that in the absence or any cogent evidence that in pursuance of the alleged agreement for recoveyance, the case land has already, been reconveyed to the original vendors and it has actually gone back to them in the course of 12 years following the registration of the disputed sale deed the learned Court of appeal below seriously erred in law in refusing preemption on a completely erroneous view of law and same has occasioned failure of justice. 

 8. Mr. Abdus Samad Miah, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite par-ties, on the other hand, submits that in the face of the concurrent findings by the learned Courts below that the disputed transfer was hit by section 96 sub-section 10(d) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as being a usufructory mortgage or a conditional sale, the impugned judgments do not suffer from any illegality or legal infirmity justying interference by this Court. 

 10. 0.P.W.1 stated in his evidence that the deed of agreement was not registered for financial reasons. From this it is evident that the parties were fully aware of the necessity and importance of registration of this valuable document witnessing an agreement for reconveyance of the case land but the fact of the agreement for re conveyance was not at all mentioned in the sale deed and it was left unregistered on unconvincing grounds. This deed of agreement dated 4.3.84 clearly mentions that the case land was sold to the pre-emptee by registered kabala. In his evidence before the court 0.P.1 Atul Chandra Roy stated that in terms of the agreement for re conveyance they agreed to reconvey the land to the vendors any time if they were paid back the consideration money. He also clearly admitted in his cross-examination that he does not know the reason why his wife her 2 sisters mortgaged the case land to the pre-emptee. In this case, none of the vendors of the sale under pre-emption has came before the court to support the defence plea. It is found that the disputed sale deed and the alleged deed of re conveyance have been written by the same scribe. The contesting opposite party placed nothing on record to satisfy the court as to what prevented the opposite parties from mentioning in the disputed sale deed the story of agreement for reconveyance and what prevented the parties from getting the so-call agreement for re conveyance registered. 

 13. In the facts, and circumstances of the case and the materials on record, I am of the view that the learned courts below clearly erred in law in disallowing pre-emption on an erroneous view regarding the real import of section 96 sub-section 10(d) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the same has occasioned failure of .justice.
